github.title: How to get a GitHub token
github.intro: Use a fine-grained personal access token so this source only sees the repository you choose.
github.step1: Open GitHub Settings, then Developer settings.
github.step2: Choose Personal access tokens, then create a fine-grained token.
github.step3: Select the repository you want Cowork to read.
github.step4: Set an expiration date, generate the token, and paste it into Access token.
github.note: For a mock connection, any token-shaped value works. In a real connector, Cowork would validate the token before saving it.

linear.title: How to get a Linear API key
linear.intro: Create a personal API key from the Linear workspace you want to browse.
linear.step1: Open Linear and switch to the target workspace.
linear.step3: Create a personal API key and copy it once it appears.
linear.step4: Paste the workspace URL and API key into the connect form.
linear.note: Keep the API key private. This mock stores only the connected source id locally, not the field values.

notion.title: Set up your Notion connection
notion.intro: Three quick stages — create an integration, share what to read, then connect. Most "no items" cases are just a missed share in stage 2.

create.title: 1. Create an integration
create.step1: Open https://www.notion.so/my-integrations and click New integration → Internal.
create.step2: Name it and, under Capabilities, enable Read content only (no write or comment access needed).
create.step3: Copy the Internal Integration Token (starts with ntn_). It isn't shown again, so keep it somewhere safe.

share.title: 2. Share pages & databases with it
share.step1: Sharing is per-item: open a top-level page (or database) you want to browse.
share.step2: Open the top-right ⋯ menu → Connections → add the integration you just created.
share.step3: Sharing a parent page includes its sub-pages; share each separate top-level page on its own.

connect.title: 3. Connect & verify
connect.step1: In the Connect tab, paste the token, pick a mount name, and press Connect Notion.
connect.step2: Shared top-level pages appear as folders. Tables inside a page show inline; standalone databases are still limited (page-focused for now).

notion.scopeShared: Only pages shared with the integration are visible
notion.note: The token is write-only here — it is never shown again. To change it, disconnect and reconnect.

s3.title: Set up your S3 connection
s3.intro: Four stages — IAM user, read-only policy, access key, connect. Use a least-privilege key scoped to just the bucket you want to browse.

user.title: 1. Create an IAM user
user.step1: Open the AWS IAM console → Users → Create user (or reuse a dedicated one, e.g. cowork-s3-readonly).
user.step2: Programmatic access is enough — no console sign-in needed. You'll add the key in stage 3.

policy.title: 2. Attach a read-only policy
policy.step1: Attach a policy scoped to just this bucket — not account-wide S3 access.
policy.step2: Allow s3:ListBucket on the bucket (arn:aws:s3:::BUCKET) and s3:GetObject on its objects (arn:aws:s3:::BUCKET/*).
policy.step3: Grant nothing else — no write or delete. Least privilege keeps a leaked key harmless.

key.title: 3. Create an access key
key.step1: In the user's Security credentials tab, create an access key for application use.
key.step2: Copy the Access key ID and Secret access key. The secret is shown only once.

connect.title: 4. Connect
connect.step1: In the Connect tab, enter the bucket, region, and the two keys, then press Connect S3.
connect.step2: For S3-compatible storage (MinIO, Cloudflare R2) set the endpoint too; use a key prefix to scope to a subfolder.

s3.note: The secret key is write-only here — it is never shown again. To change it, disconnect and reconnect. Prefer a least-privilege, read-only key.
